question: How does a calm melody carry both consolation and unease?
intro: After the stormy B minor first movement, the symphony’s second and last movement is an E major song in 3/8 with a plaintive second theme in the minor. Listen for the horns and bassoons at the start, the clarinet and oboe that carry the second theme, and the woodwinds’ distant A♭ major near the end.

B · the minor second theme and closing theme
A′ · the first theme returns

sections.label: Coda · the cadential figure and the A♭ major

cues.title: Horns and bassoons, plucked basses
cues.text: The Andante con moto opens in E major with a two-bar cadential figure for bassoons and horns, pianissimo, over plucked basses. The strings then begin the theme, and the figure comes back between phrases. It is a movement of answering voices.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #73284, p. 19) shows bassoons and horns pp in the first bars with basses pizzicato, and the strings entering in the third bar. The report’s opening level is −44.9 dB at 0:00, rising to −23.5 dB by 0:10; no entry is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Voices in counterpoint
cues.text: Wikipedia describes the lyrical first theme as introduced by the horns, low strings, brass and high strings in counterpoint. Listen for the long arcs in the upper strings against the cellos’ moving line below.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article describes the opening theme and its scoring. The report shows the theme held at a steady, quiet level, −19.2 to −20.7 dB at 0:30–0:40, with 1.2–1.8 attacks per second and the key estimate moving from E major at 0:30 to B major at 0:35. The score (IMSLP #73284, p. 19) shows violins and viola in long phrases against a moving cello line in the early bars; no phrase is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A loud turn towards B major
cues.text: Around 1:10 the first theme builds to a forte and the key estimate settles on B major, the dominant. The loudest window of the section is near 1:30. The tune is not left behind: it carries the surge.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:04 (novelty 0.61); local key reads B major at 1:10–1:30 (r 0.76–0.90) with the level at −10.1 dB at 1:20 and −9.9 dB at 1:30. Key estimates confirm a region, not a chord.

cues.title: Hanslick’s verdict
cues.text: Eduard Hanslick, reviewing the 1865 premiere, found the Andante broader than the first movement, with hints of complaint or irritation, like musical thunder clouds. He was fascinated by the tone colour from a few horn figures and a clarinet or oboe solo.
cues.evidence: Hanslick’s review is quoted in Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article (“Reception”): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).

cues.title: Four notes before the minor
cues.text: At about 2:22 the first violins quietly spell out the tonic chord of C♯ minor in four unharmonised notes, the relative minor. They are the hinge between the calm first theme and the plaintive second.
cues.evidence: One of the strongest boundaries of the movement is 2:22 (novelty 0.84); the local key reads C♯ minor at 2:30 and 2:40 (r 0.79, 0.84). The four notes are Wikipedia’s description; they are not timed.

cues.title: The clarinet, then the oboe
cues.text: About 2:42 the solo clarinet begins the second theme in C♯ minor. The oboe then continues it in C♯ major, an example of the major and minor juxtaposed that Schubert loves. Listen for the change of colour on the same melody.
cues.evidence: Local key reads C♯ minor at 2:30, 2:40 and 3:00 (r 0.79–0.84) and C♯ major at 3:20–3:40 (r 0.87–0.96), and an A♭ major reading at 3:10 (0.72), a separate estimate from the C♯ major that follows; a recurrence analysis matches 162.5–192.0 s with 469.0–498.5 s four semitones lower (C♯ to A, a major third).

cues.title: A short score survived
cues.text: A complete short score of the second movement survives among Schubert’s papers, preserved by his brother Ferdinand, a schoolteacher. So does a scherzo, nearly finished at the piano but orchestrated for only two pages. Nothing survives of a fourth movement.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article, “Early history” and “Third and fourth movements”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).

cues.title: The loud closing theme
cues.text: From about 3:45 the whole orchestra plays a dramatic closing theme, loud at 3:45 and 3:50. It returns to C♯ minor and then ends in D♭ major, which is C♯ major spelt another way.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −20.2 dB at 3:40 to −10.6 dB at 3:45 and −10.7 dB at 3:50, with a local key of C♯ minor at 3:50–4:00 (r 0.66–0.70); a boundary at 4:08 (0.54). The key outcome is Wikipedia’s description.

cues.title: Wandering back to E major
cues.text: A short transition now leads back to the tonic. The key estimates pass through D major, G major and C major, then arrive at E major around 5:20. Listen for the harmony drifting without a firm landing until the first theme returns.
cues.evidence: Local key reads D major at 4:10–4:30 (r 0.75–0.82), G major at 4:40 (0.75), C major at 4:50–5:00 (0.79–0.82) and E major from 5:20 (0.73–0.84); boundary at 5:12 (0.63). Wikipedia calls the transition short; these are estimates only.

cues.title: The first theme again
cues.text: About 5:14 the first theme returns in E major. The recording matches the opening closely from this point for a long stretch, which shows how faithfully the recapitulation repeats it.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 12.5–27.0 s with 327.0–341.5 s and several other opening excerpts at an offset of about 310–314 s, with no transposition (similarity 0.93–0.95); boundary at 5:12 (0.63).

cues.title: B major again, then E
cues.text: Near 6:20 the recapitulated first theme reaches B major with a forte, as it did at 1:10. The key estimate returns to E major soon after. The two halves of the movement mirror each other.
cues.evidence: Local key reads B major at 6:20–6:30 (r 0.88–0.89) with −8.5 dB at 6:30 and E major at 6:40 (r 0.93); a boundary at 6:16 (0.66). A recurrence analysis matches 70.0–83.5 s with 380.5–394.0 s (no transposition, similarity 0.95); the earlier B major region is at 1:10–1:30.

cues.title: Three sides of shellac
cues.text: The symphony was recorded on 28 and 30 April 1927 and issued on three Victor discs, 6663–6665, six sides for two movements. The Internet Archive transfer presents each movement as one file, so side changes lie inside it, though nothing identifies where.
cues.evidence: Pristine Classical’s notes give matrices CVE 29052-6 to 29057-7, the dates 28 and 30 April 1927 and first issue on Victor 6663–6665 (https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc483). Three discs make six sides for two movements; the Bolig discography lists three parts (sides) for each movement (https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf), and the join points inside each file are not timed.

cues.title: A minor, not E minor
cues.text: At about 7:49 the second theme returns, now in A minor, the subdominant minor, rather than the expected E minor. Wikipedia notes that the oboe begins it and the clarinet continues, the reverse of the exposition.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 162.5–192.0 s with 469.0–498.5 s transposed four semitones down (C♯ to A; similarity 0.91); local key reads A minor at 7:40 and 7:50 (r 0.81, 0.83). The change of soloists is Wikipedia’s description.

cues.title: The loudest windows
cues.text: The closing theme returns for the full orchestra, and the recording’s loudest windows fall between 8:50 and 9:10. Compare it with the first closing theme near 3:50: here it is much louder.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows are 8:55, 8:50, 9:05, 9:10 and 9:00 (−5.4 dB at 8:50, −7.3 dB at 9:00 and 9:10) against −10.7 dB at 3:50.

cues.title: The coda begins
cues.text: From about 9:30 the coda starts, as Wikipedia describes it, with a new theme that extends the two-bar cadential figure that opened the movement. The level eases: the long climax is over.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −7.3 dB at 9:10 to −18.6 dB at 10:00; B major reads at 9:30–9:50 (r 0.87–0.90). The coda’s structure is Wikipedia’s description and its start is estimated, not aligned; the strongest boundary comes later at 10:36.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A♭ major, a distant light
cues.text: At 10:36 clarinets and bassoons, supported by the bass trombone, restate the first theme in A♭ major over very quiet strings, a long way from E major: the strongest boundary of the movement. A pause at 10:30 prepares it. The harmony shifts as though a window had opened on another room.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 10:36 (novelty 1.00), with a quiet window at 10:30 (−30.1 dB) and local key A♭ major at 10:40 (r 0.92); boundaries at 10:24 (0.84), 10:50 (0.54), 10:56 (0.78) and 11:00 (0.88). Wikipedia describes the woodwind restatement in A♭ major; the clarinet, bassoon and bass trombone scoring, with the flute and oboe resting, is read from the score (IMSLP #73284, printed p. 31).

cues.title: The motto leads home
cues.text: The laconic triadic motto in the first violins appears again, and by about 11:10 the key estimate is E major once more. A last transformation of the first theme follows.
cues.evidence: Local key reads E major at 11:10 and 11:40 (r 0.91, 0.87), with levels −17.4 dB at 11:10 and −14.6 dB at 11:40; boundaries at 10:56 (0.78) and 11:00 (0.88). The motto and the final transformation are Wikipedia’s description.

cues.title: Why only two
cues.text: Scholars disagree about why Schubert stopped. A fourth movement in B minor would normally have followed; some propose that the Rosamunde entr’acte in B minor was meant for it. The symphony ends in E major, not the B minor in which it began, which tradition would not have accepted.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Symphony No. 8 article, “Third and fourth movements” and the opening discussion of Brian Newbould’s theory: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert). The article presents the Rosamunde link as circumstantial.

transitions.title: Four notes open the minor
transitions.how: After the first theme’s cadence in E major, the first violins quietly spell out the tonic chord of C♯ minor in four unharmonised notes, the relative minor. The clarinet then takes up a plaintive melody in C♯ minor, and the oboe continues it in C♯ major: major and minor alternate over the same tune. No pivot chord is needed, because the relative minor shares the key signature with E major.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 2:22 (novelty 0.84); C♯ minor reads from 2:30, A♭ major at 3:10 and C♯ major at 3:20–3:40. The four notes, the clarinet and the oboe are Wikipedia’s description; the key signature is on printed p. 19 of IMSLP #73284 (four sharps).

transitions.title: D♭ becomes C♯, and E major returns
transitions.how: The loud closing theme returns to C♯ minor but ends in D♭ major, the enharmonic equivalent of C♯ major. A short transition then brings the music back to E major, and the first theme returns. The recording’s key estimates wander through D, G and C major on the way, which suggests a sequence of descending fifths. The return is recognised by the theme and the key together.
transitions.evidence: Local key reads C♯ minor at 3:50–4:00, D major at 4:10–4:30, G major at 4:40, C major at 4:50–5:00 and E major from 5:20; boundary at 5:12 (0.63); a recurrence analysis matches the opening excerpts with an offset of about 312 s. The enharmonic close in D♭ major is Wikipedia’s description.

transitions.title: The second theme drops to A minor
transitions.to: B′ · second theme in A minor
transitions.how: In the recapitulation the second theme comes back not in E minor, the tonic minor, but in A minor, the subdominant minor. The oboe begins it and the clarinet continues, reversing the roles of the exposition. Schubert shifts the theme down a major third, four semitones, from C♯ minor to A minor, so the minor shade is darker and lower than before.
transitions.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 162.5–192.0 s with 469.0–498.5 s transposed four semitones down; local key reads A minor at 7:40 and 7:50. The oboe and clarinet roles and the subdominant minor are Wikipedia’s description.

transitions.title: The cadential figure grows into a coda
transitions.from: B′ · second theme in A minor
transitions.how: After the loudest passage of the movement, the closing theme gives way to the coda. Its first theme is simply an extension of the two-bar cadential figure that opened the movement, and the music comes back to its starting point. The level falls, and later a pause at 10:30 prepares the distant A♭ major of the clarinets and bassoons.
transitions.evidence: Loudest windows at 8:50–9:10 then level falls to −18.6 dB at 10:00; a quiet window at 10:30 (−30.1 dB) before the boundary at 10:36. The coda’s structure is Wikipedia’s description and its start is estimated rather than aligned.

timeline.note: Bassoons and horns sound the two-bar cadential figure over plucked basses.
The strings take up the first theme in long phrases, with winds answering.
The first violins quietly spell out the C♯ minor chord.
The solo clarinet sings the second theme in C♯ minor.
The solo oboe continues it in C♯ major.
The first theme returns in E major.
The second theme in A minor: oboe first, then clarinet.
The closing theme again, the loudest passage of the recording.
Clarinets and bassoons, supported by the bass trombone, restate the first theme in A♭ major over very quiet strings.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 28 and 30 April 1927: part 1 on 28 April, parts 2 and 3 on 30 April
fields.note: Bolig dates CVE-29055 (part 1) to 28 April 1927 and CVE-29056 and CVE-29057 (parts 2 and 3) to 30 April 1927; the Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days for the symphony. Bolig calls the movement “Allegro con moto”; the usual marking is Andante con moto.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.

fields.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29055, take 7 (Bolig) or take 6 (Pristine); CVE-29056, take 7; CVE-29057, take 7
fields.note: The two discographic sources agree on the matrices and on takes 7 for CVE-29056 and CVE-29057 but differ on the take of CVE-29055. Neither can be checked against a label image here, and the DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 11:55; Pristine’s own restoration runs 12:00, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.

fields.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item carries a CC0 licence URL declared by the uploader, which is not treated as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
